name: Jamaica
summary: A former Spanish and British colony built on sugar and slavery, independent in 1962; birthplace of reggae.

terrain.value: A mountainous interior, with the Blue Mountains rising to 2,256 m and the limestone Cockpit Country, ringed by coastal plains, beaches and harbours.

climate.value: Tropical, hot and humid on the coast and cooler in the mountains; rains peak around May and October, and hurricanes come from June to November.

resources.value: Bauxite and alumina, fertile land for sugar, bananas and Blue Mountain coffee, and beaches that draw tourists.

disasters.value: Hurricanes such as Gilbert (1988), Ivan (2004) and Melissa (2025), along with floods, droughts and occasional earthquakes.

population.value: 2,824,913 in a 2024 estimate; 2,774,538 at the 2022 census.

urbanisation.value: More than half the people live in towns; Kingston, the capital and main port, and Montego Bay, the tourist hub, are the largest, with Portmore and Spanish Town nearby.

disease.value: Outbreaks of dengue, chikungunya (2014) and Zika, alongside rising rates of diabetes and heart disease.

migration.value: Large diaspora in the UK and US (Windrush).

economicBase.value: Tourism, about 4.3 million visitors a year, is the largest foreign-exchange earner; Jamaica is the fifth-largest bauxite exporter.

tradeRoutes.value: Kingston’s deep natural harbour is a major container port; bauxite and alumina are shipped from south-coast ports, and Montego Bay handles cruise ships and flights.

wealth.value: An upper-middle-income country, but with slow growth from the 1970s to the 2010s and heavy public debt for much of that time.

moneyAndTax.value: The Jamaican dollar, introduced in 1969 to replace the pound; revenue comes from income tax and a general consumption tax (GCT).

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy with the British monarch as head of state.

keyRulers.value: Alexander Bustamante founded the Jamaica Labour Party and was first prime minister at independence on 6 August 1962; Norman Manley led the People’s National Party; Michael Manley led the PNP to win in 1972 and Edward Seaga the JLP in 1980.

succession.value: Prime ministers come from the party that wins parliamentary elections, held at least every five years; power has alternated between the JLP and PNP.

institutions.value: A two-chamber Parliament (an elected House of Representatives and an appointed Senate), the governor-general, the courts and the Jamaica Defence Force.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Jamaica Defence Force (formed 1962), with army, coast guard and air wing units, used mainly for internal security and disaster relief.

majorWars.value: No wars as an independent state. Earlier: the First Maroon War (1728–1740) ended in stalemate and treaties, the Second (1795–96) ended with Maroons expelled to Nova Scotia and Sierra Leone, and the Morant Bay rebellion of 1865 led by Paul Bogle was suppressed by Governor Eyre.

territoryChange.value: No changes since independence; the country also includes small offshore cays such as the Pedro and Morant Cays.

alliancesRivals.value: A Commonwealth member and founding member of CARICOM (1973), with close ties to the US, UK and Canada; Manley’s government was friendly with Cuba in the 1970s.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of the West Indies at Mona, the University of Technology and teacher-training colleges; literacy rose after independence.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and toll highways such as Highway 2000, buses and route taxis, and Norman Manley (Kingston) and Sangster (Montego Bay) international airports.

languageWriting.value: English is the official language; most people also speak Jamaican Patois (Patwa), an English-based creole with West African influences.

artsArchitecture.value: Ska, rocksteady, reggae (Bob Marley) and dancehall music, Edna Manley’s sculpture, and Georgian buildings in towns such as Falmouth.

socialStructure.value: Mostly people of African descent, with smaller groups of mixed, Indian, Chinese, European and Middle Eastern descent; class divides follow wealth and colour.

sharedIdentity.value: The motto “Out of many, one people” reflects a shared Jamaican identity built on music, sport, food and Afro-Caribbean culture.

dailyLife.value: Many live in towns in concrete houses; meals include ackee and saltfish, jerk chicken, rice and peas, and patties.

neighbours.value: Cuba to the north, Haiti to the east across the Jamaica Channel, and the Cayman Islands to the northwest.

ideasReligions.value: Rastafari, which began in Jamaica in the 1930s, and the Pan-Africanism of Marcus Garvey, named a national hero in 1969.

colonisation.value: England conquered the island in 1655; a British colony until independence on 6 August 1962.

riseSignals.value: Full independence on 6 August 1962, after the Federation of the West Indies (1958–62).

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge. The page does not mention reggae's 1970s fame beyond calling Jamaica its birthplace; it says tourism and mining are the leading foreign-exchange earners.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still an independent country, a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state since independence on 6 August 1962.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
